title: Dependency Injection Pattern
oneLiner: Supplies a class's dependencies from outside instead of letting it construct them itself, making it swappable and testable.

hero.name: The Provider
hero.catchphrase: Don't build your own tools. I'll hand you exactly what you need.
hero.power: Supplies a class with the dependencies it needs from the outside, instead of the class constructing them itself, making swapping and testing trivial.
hero.weakness: Heavy framework magic — auto-wiring via reflection or annotations — can make it genuinely hard to trace where a given dependency actually came from.
hero.origin: The Provider appeared after `OrderService`'s constructor directly did `new StripeGateway()`, making it impossible to test order logic without a real (or heavily mocked) Stripe connection.

story.problem: `OrderService`'s constructor calls `new StripeGateway()` directly. Every test that touches OrderService needs a real (or awkwardly mocked) Stripe connection, even for logic that has nothing to do with payments.
story.solution: The Provider changes `OrderService` to accept a `PaymentGateway` through its constructor instead of building one itself. Tests pass in a fake; production code passes in the real Stripe gateway.
story.result: OrderService no longer knows or cares which payment gateway it's using. Tests inject a fake in microseconds; swapping providers means passing a different implementation, with zero changes to OrderService itself.

before: A class constructs its own dependencies internally
Testing requires the real dependency or complex mocking
Swapping an implementation means editing the class itself
after: Dependencies are supplied from outside, through the constructor
Testing just injects a lightweight fake
Swapping an implementation means passing a different argument

panels.label: The Problem
panels.caption: A unit test for order-total calculation fails because it can't reach the real Stripe API in CI.
panels.speaker: Developer
panels.dialogue: I'm testing tax math and it's failing because OrderService insists on constructing a real Stripe connection internally.

panels.label: The Hero Arrives
panels.caption: The Provider appears holding out a tray of ready-made tools, offering them instead of letting anyone build their own.
panels.speaker: The Provider
panels.dialogue: Don't construct your dependencies yourself. Accept them from outside — I'll hand you exactly what you need, real or fake.

panels.label: Pattern Power
panels.caption: OrderService's constructor now accepts a PaymentGateway parameter instead of constructing one internally.
panels.speaker: The Provider
panels.dialogue: Production hands you the real Stripe gateway. Tests hand you a fake. OrderService itself never changes either way.

panels.label: The Result
panels.caption: The tax-math test now runs in milliseconds with a fake gateway, no network calls involved.
panels.speaker: Developer
panels.dialogue: The test runs instantly now with a fake gateway. Zero network calls needed to test tax math.

useWhen: A class depends on something that's expensive, external, or varies by environment (a payment gateway, a database, an API client).
You want to unit test a class's logic without needing its real dependencies to be available.
You want to swap an implementation (a different payment provider, a mock database) without editing the class that uses it.
avoidWhen: The dependency is a simple, stable value with no need for swapping or mocking (like a math utility function).
A full DI framework's auto-wiring machinery would add more indirection than the app's size actually justifies.
The class and its dependency are so tightly coupled by design that injecting alternatives would never make sense.
commonMistakes: Reaching for a heavy DI framework with reflection-based auto-wiring for a small app where plain constructor injection would be simpler and more traceable.
Injecting so many dependencies into one constructor that it signals the class is doing too much and should be split up.
Using a Service Locator instead of real injection, hiding a class's true dependencies inside its method bodies instead of its constructor.
Forgetting that DI is about WHO supplies the dependency, not a specific framework — you can do genuine dependency injection with zero framework at all, just passing arguments.
explanation.realWorldExample: Spring's `@Autowired`, Angular's constructor-based DI, and any codebase that passes dependencies as constructor arguments instead of `new`-ing them internally are Dependency Injection in practice.

conversation.speaker: Mentor
conversation.message: Do I need a DI framework to do this?

conversation.speaker: The Provider
conversation.message: Not at all — the simplest form of me is just passing arguments to a constructor. Frameworks automate wiring for large systems, but the core idea works with zero framework at all.

conversation.speaker: Mentor
conversation.message: When does DI actually hurt readability?

conversation.speaker: The Provider
conversation.message: When auto-wiring hides WHERE a dependency comes from — annotations resolving things behind the scenes make it hard to trace, at a glance, what's actually being injected and why.

codeBattle.scenario: Your `EmailService` constructs its own SMTP client internally, and every test that touches any code calling EmailService ends up trying to send a real email, slowing down and flaking your test suite.
codeBattle.question: Which hero should you call?
codeBattle.explanation: The Provider lets EmailService accept its SMTP client from outside, so tests can inject a fake client instead of sending real emails.

quiz.question: What does Dependency Injection change about how a class gets its dependencies?
options: Dependencies are supplied from outside instead of being constructed internally by the class
The class must always use a Singleton for every dependency
Dependencies are looked up from a global registry by name
The class can no longer have any dependencies at all
quiz.answer: Dependencies are supplied from outside instead of being constructed internally by the class
quiz.explanation: Externalizing dependency creation is the entire premise of Dependency Injection.

quiz.question: What's the simplest form of Dependency Injection?
options: Passing a dependency as a constructor argument, with no framework required
Using a heavy reflection-based auto-wiring framework
Storing the dependency in a global variable
Hardcoding the dependency directly in the class
quiz.answer: Passing a dependency as a constructor argument, with no framework required
quiz.explanation: DI's core idea works with plain constructor arguments — frameworks just automate wiring at scale.

quiz.question: How does Dependency Injection improve testability?
options: Tests can supply lightweight fake dependencies instead of needing the real ones
It removes the need for any tests at all
It makes every test require a real database connection
It prevents classes from having any dependencies
quiz.answer: Tests can supply lightweight fake dependencies instead of needing the real ones
quiz.explanation: Injecting a fake in place of a real, expensive dependency is exactly what makes fast, isolated unit tests possible.

quiz.question: How does Dependency Injection differ from Service Locator?
options: DI supplies dependencies explicitly (often via constructor); Service Locator hides them inside method bodies via a lookup call
They are identical patterns with different names
Service Locator requires a constructor; DI forbids constructors
DI can only be used with databases
quiz.answer: DI supplies dependencies explicitly (often via constructor); Service Locator hides them inside method bodies via a lookup call
quiz.explanation: DI makes dependencies visible at construction time; Service Locator hides them until a lookup happens somewhere inside the class.
